name: Guanche
confidence_why: Guanche is extinct and survives only in Hispanicized place names and chronicle glosses, and every source that touches on its stress — Trapero and Santana Martel 2018, Ballester 2003, Acosta Armas 2017 and Bute 1891 — offers only word-by-word conjectures and island-level tendencies (proparoxytones on El Hierro, final stress on La Gomera) rather than a rule, with Acosta Armas 2017 saying outright that the stressed syllable of a Guanche word can hardly be known.

'Estudio', cap. 11 'Una gramática elemental del bereber de aplicación al guanche', §11.1 'El sistema fonológico'; cap. 15 'La escritura de los topónimos guanches', §15.3 'Propuesta de escritura basada en la oralidad', párrafo 'La acentuación'.

catalog_quote: Acento. El acento prosódico se constituye en el español en una marca fonológica fuerte [...]. Por eso suponemos que el acento que en la actualidad conservan los topónimos guanches, tal como los conocemos en la oralidad, es más fiel al original guanche que las vocales y las consonantes que los constituyen. [...] Por eso llaman tanto la atención los topónimos que tienen dos o más variantes con cambio acentual, como Áfite / Afite, Ajifio / Ajifío, Anjúa / Anjua, Atosar / Atósar, Bedio / Bedío, Beñamo / Béñamo, Birama / Bírama, Brasía / Brasia, Eris / Erís, Güigüí / Guguy, Güime / Goíme, Gusano / Gúsano y bastantes más. Esdrújulos en El Hierro. Igualmente llama la atención la larga serie de voces con acentuación esdrújula que se conserva en El Hierro, siendo esta prosodia tan extraña a la morfología del español común y popular, y tanto en voces que son topónimos, como Arétique, Asánaque, Bérote, Ícona, Ícota, Itámote, Mancáfete, Quésquere, Sísaque, Téjena, Tembárgena, Tésera o Tamájesa, como en voces que siguen teniendo la condición de apelativos [...]: cómbaca, ómana, jórana, mástuca, mérusa, pípana, etc. [...] Agudos en La Gomera. Si en El Hierro son las palabras esdrújulas las que llaman la atención, en La Gomera son los topónimos que acaban en una vocal acentuada, mayoritariamente en é pero también en á, tales como Aradá, Chejeré, Chelé, Cheselé, Chigadá [...]. También los hay en la toponimia de Tenerife, pero no en igual número ni proporción
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Accent. Prosodic accent is a strong phonological mark in Spanish [...]. We therefore assume that the accent that Guanche toponyms keep today, as we know them from oral tradition, is more faithful to the Guanche original than the vowels and consonants that make them up. [...] Equally striking is the long series of words with antepenultimate (esdrújula) stress preserved in El Hierro, a prosody so foreign to the morphology of common, popular Spanish [...]. If in El Hierro it is the antepenult-stressed words that stand out, in La Gomera it is the toponyms that end in a stressed vowel, mostly in -é but also in -á.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is stated or recoverable. Guanche is extinct and known only through Hispanicised toponyms, anthroponyms and a few phrases; the authors hold that the stress of surviving oral toponyms is probably original, and that alongside the (Spanish-like, unremarked) penultimate majority there are island-specific clusters of antepenultimate stress (El Hierro: Arétique, Bérote, Itámote, Tembárgena; colour terms cómbaca, ómana, mástuca) and final stress (La Gomera: Aradá, Chejeré, Chelé; fewer in Tenerife: Fañabé, Guiné), plus many doublets differing only in stress (Atosar/Atósar, Beñamo/Béñamo). Ballester 2003 (pp. 12-14) independently reconstructs many proparoxytones and 'muchas más formas no oxítonas' ending in -d/-n/-r than Castilian allows (Güímar, tagóror, Jinámar); Acosta Armas 2017 (p. 23 n. 24) states the tonic syllable of a guanchismo can hardly be known because the chronicles do not mark accent. Net: stress position lexically variable in the surviving corpus and not reducible to a rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Doublets with accent shift (Áfite/Afite, Ajifio/Ajifío, Anjúa/Anjua, Atosar/Atósar, Bedio/Bedío, Beñamo/Béñamo, Birama/Bírama, Brasía/Brasia, Eris/Erís, Güime/Goíme, Gusano/Gúsano); §15 warns that written/cartographic forms carry many accent errors (Jinámar GC vs Jinama EH; Julan not Julán; Marsagán, Tesén, Arguineguín, Mogán). Ballester adds the caveat that unmarked accent in old Castilian spelling may have produced spelling-pronunciations.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word accent of Guanche-origin toponyms and appellatives as pronounced today in Canarian Spanish oral tradition (citation forms), used as a proxy for the extinct language; not phrase-level. Island differences (El Hierro antepenult, La Gomera/Tenerife final) may reflect inter-island dialect differences of the pre-Hispanic language(s).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern the pre-Hispanic language(s) of the Canary Islands (Glottolog guan1277 'Guanche', iso gnc, used in the broad sense for all seven islands, not only Tenerife) as reflected in Guanche-origin toponyms and appellatives surviving in present-day Canarian Spanish; the accent observations are island-specific (antepenultimate cluster in El Hierro, final-stress cluster in La Gomera and to a lesser degree Tenerife), which the authors treat as possibly reflecting inter-island dialect differences. No living speakers; evidence is 15th-17th c. chronicle spellings (mostly without accent marks; Espinosa 1594 marks some) plus modern oral toponymy.

new_statements.quote: [p. 555, Teil IV § 315] Die Betonung auf der letzten Silbe wäre eine Kostbarkeit für uns, aber sie kommt zuerst bei VR vor, in dessen Erstdruck in spanischen und Eingeborenenworten die Akzente ganz willkürlich und unberechtigt gesetzt sind. [p. 674, Teil V § 86 mulagua] Der Wechsel von Formen mit Erhaltung oder mit Ausfall des Vokals der vorletzten Silbe betrachten wir als Beweis dafür, daß das Wort auf der zweiten Silbe betont war und daß genau so wie im Berber., der Vokal der nachtonigen Silbe zum Murmelvokal wurde und geneigt war völlig auszufallen [...]. [pp. 761-2, Teil V § 315] ... weil berber. der Artikel und Präfixe gern den Ton an sich ziehen
new_statements.translation: [p. 555] Stress on the last syllable would be a treasure for us, but it first appears in VR [Viera y Clavijo], in whose first printing the accents on Spanish and native words are set quite arbitrarily and without justification. [p. 674] We regard the alternation of forms that keep or drop the vowel of the penultimate syllable as proof that the word was stressed on the second syllable and that, exactly as in Berber, the vowel of the post-tonic syllable became a murmured vowel and tended to drop out entirely [...]. [pp. 761-2] ... since in Berber the article and prefixes like to draw the accent onto themselves

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'undetermined' record (Trapero 2018: the accent of the toponyms is the most faithful remnant, but many accent doublets; long series of proparoxytones on El Hierro, oxytones on La Gomera). Wölfel adds, from the historical corpus rather than modern toponymy: the accent marks of the 18th-19th c. compilers are worthless as evidence of the tonic syllable; stress position is recoverable only word by word from vowel syncope, and where he reads it it falls on the penult/second syllable with Berber-like post-tonic reduction, with prefixes able to attract the accent; his planned accent chapter (VI §§ 5-6) was never. Díaz Alayón & Castillo 2002 (held by the project, read)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work states no rule for Guanche ('kanarisch') word stress. Its systematic phonology, planned as Teil VI Kap. 1 'Die Lautlehre des Kanarischen: Vokalismus' with § 5 'Betonte Vokale' and § 6 'Akzent und Vokalelysion', exists only as a table of planned paragraph headings (pp. 903-906): Wölfel died in 1963 and the compilers printed the outline without text (Nachwort des Bearbeiters, p. 907: §§ 1-75 were to draw the phonetic and grammatical conclusions from Teile IV-V). What Teile IV-V say about accent is entry by entry: (a) the written accents of the compilers (Viera y Clavijo, Olive, Chil, Millares) are set arbitrarily and are no evidence for the tonic syllable ('Auf VRs Akzentuierung ist nichts zu geben', p. 751; 'Ob der Akzent bei MIL wirklich die Tonstelle bezeichnet, wissen wir nicht', p. 852); (b) for individual names Wölfel infers the stressed syllable from syncope/reduction of neighbouring vowels, e.g. mulagua/amaluige stressed on the second syllable with Berber-like reduction of the post-tonic vowel (p. 674), guergue/teneguerguera stressed on the penult (p. 804), magado perhaps mágodo with a murmured medial vowel (p. 545), banot/vonode 'Betonung banót, vonóde' (p. 547); (c) two working generalizations: loss of a final consonant (-r, -s) occurred only in an unstressed final syllable (pp. 723, 873), and, as in Berber, article and prefixes tend to attract the accent, which can syncopate the first stem vowel (pp. 761-762). No statement that stress was fixed, free, or absent.
new_statements.exceptions: no rule, hence no exceptions; Wölfel notes modern island-Spanish accent shifts in surviving toponyms (p. 712 bentáyga: 'Hat hier in der inselspanischen Aussprache der Akzent den Diphthong von der unbetonten Endsilbe auf die betonte vorletzte gezogen?') and accent doublets in Lanzarote names (pp. 665-666 haría/háría: 'denselben Widerspruch der Akzentuierung')
new_statements.identity_note: Monumenta Linguae Canariae covers the recorded pre-Hispanic language material of all seven Canary Islands ('das Kanarische'), entry by entry with the island named (Tenerife, Gran Canaria, La Palma, El Hierro/Ferro, La Gomera, Lanzarote, Fuerteventura), from 14th-19th c. written sources plus modern toponymy; 'Guanche' in the catalog sense (guan1277) = this whole insular corpus, not only Tenerife. The accent remarks quoted concern names from El Hierro (esero), La Gomera (mulagua), Tenerife (Güímar, guergue, magado, banot) and Gran Canaria (gaineguín).
